html:
The Watt steam engine was James Watt's improved steam engine, patented in 1769, whose separate condenser made steam power efficient enough to drive mills and factories. It became a driving force of the Industrial Revolution.

Steam engines already existed. Thomas Newcomen's engine of 1712 pumped water from mines, but it heated and cooled the same cylinder on every stroke and burned huge amounts of coal. Watt, an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, saw the waste while repairing a model of it. His answer was to condense the steam in a separate chamber, so the main cylinder could stay hot. That cut fuel use by about three quarters.

From 1775 Watt worked with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton, who supplied money, skilled workers and sales.

  • The first engines were sold to pump water out of Cornish tin and copper mines.
  • In the 1780s Watt added gearing to turn a shaft, a double acting cylinder and a governor to control speed. Now the engine could power machines.
  • Cotton mills, breweries, ironworks and flour mills bought them, and factories no longer had to sit by a river. The cotton revolution ran on them.

Watt kept to low pressure steam, thinking high pressure too dangerous. Others, once his patent expired in 1800, built lighter high pressure engines, which could move themselves: the locomotives of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway and the steamships that followed. The watt, the unit of power, is named after him.
